en: The Refutation of the Whole (Avayavinirākaraṇa), composed by the scholar Aśoka. Homage to Samantabhadra!
No such excellence of practice has been performed by me, nor has such learning been acquired;
yet, if I now desire to compose even a mere fragment of meaning despite my own fickleness,
let the wise examine all that I have said, having considered this very fact.
For generally, the minds of parents are indeed delighted by the [actions] of their child.
Whatever possesses the superimposition of contradictory properties is not a single entity,
just like an object such as a jar.

And since an object such as a gross blue thing possesses the superimposition of contradictory properties, this is the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).

In this context, the subject (*dharmin*) is the gross, blue object currently being perceived; and since it is established by experience and remains uncontradicted, its status as established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa-siddha*) refutes the charge of the reason’s lack of a substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
[Objection: But surely you yourselves maintain that the whole (*avayavin*) is non-existent; how then can it be established by direct perception?
We do not accept the "whole" (*avayavin*) here as the subject (*dharmin*), but rather the object that appears as something gross, such as blue and so forth.
In that case, the unity of the whole would not be negated on the grounds of its association with contradictory properties.
If this is so, then what, according to you, is the "whole"?
If it is argued that [the object] is a single entity inhering in multiple parts,
is that [entity] different or non-different from the gross blue and so forth that appear?
It cannot first of all be different.
Because it is accepted as being an object of perception;
and nothing else appears apart from the manifest, gross, blue object. If it were non-different [from that object], then...
If its unity is rejected, how can the unity of the whole (avayavin) remain unrefuted?
But surely, if the object appearing [in cognition] is not the subject (dharmin) in the form of a whole,
what then will remain as its established form?

It is said: the coarse blue form appearing [in cognition] is a nature established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa-siddha*), which remains even when the existence of a composite whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted.
Nor should it be thought thus:
For those who maintain that [objects] are mere aggregations of atoms, there is no gross form whatsoever that could exist as a well-known subject (*dharmin*).
For even if one does not admit a composite whole (*avayavin*), who can deny a gross object consisting of multiple partless entities if it is accepted?
It might be thought: "How could partless atoms appear in a gross form in direct perception?"
"The claim that there is a contradiction between the gross and the subtle is also not tenable;
for it is precisely atoms, arising by excluding the space occupied by other forms and appearing in conjunction with one another, that manifest as having spatial extension."
Furthermore, "grossness" consists in occupying an extended space.

As for what was said regarding the contradiction between the gross and the subtle: do you intend to assert that the contradiction lies in the production of partless entities which exclude the space occupied by other forms, or in their appearing as a single cognitive manifestation while being mutually associated?
If this [multiplicity] is contradictory, why is the gross form (*sthūlākāra*) not also contradictory?

For this very reason, when many partless [atoms] appear in a single cognition, the gross form—which exists as a property of the appearance at the time of its manifestation—is not real, because it is absent in each individual atom.
If you then argue that the object is therefore not gross before or after the appearance, [we reply: no.
Even then, it is not so, because the capacity for manifestation is possible; for it is precisely when atoms are accumulated that they become capable of manifesting.
And when they are capable of manifesting, they are gross.
As for the one who says that when many partless [atoms] manifest, there must necessarily be something manifested in between them as well:
If there were no manifestation of the intervals between them, they would not appear as mutually distinct;
and if the distinct intervals were not manifested, the mass would become a mere atom.
Yet we do not perceive any interval being manifested.
Therefore, this [object], being a single, continuous, and partless entity, must consist of many parts;
however, it is rather a single gross entity itself.
This too must be stated in the same manner.
Is there an interval consisting of another atom of a different kind,
or rather a connection with empty space?
In that regard, a connection with empty space, being a non-entity, is not within the range of sensory perception.
For in that case, since it arises through the power of the object, it is logical that the object itself appears.

But how could something of a different class, which is perceivable by another sense organ, appear in a cognition produced by a different sense organ? Since it is not its object, we do not know by what means it could possibly appear.
Furthermore, as for what is said— that if the intermediate spaces were not illuminated, the distinct objects would not appear as isolated—
it must be considered whether their "intermediate" nature consists of isolation (*viveka*) or of being empty of the form of another (*pararūpa-śūnyatā*).
Upon investigation, however, we perceive the isolation (*viveka*) of things as being precisely their emptiness of other-natures (*pararūpa-śūnyatā*).
Since these appearing entities are empty of other-natures, how could they not manifest as isolated?
But surely, the gross form does not belong to each individual atom.
Therefore, it must be accepted that [the gross form] arises from those [atoms] combined.

Just as the yellow form, which is impossible for blue atoms individually, is not seen even when they are many, so too how could a gross form, being impossible for each individual [atom], exist in many?
It has been stated in this regard: "A gross form is not contradictory for partless [atoms]. However, a yellow form is contradictory to a blue one.
Therefore, even when there are many [atoms] bearing a blue form which is contradictory to yellow, how could a yellow form arise?
Thus, a gross form is not at all contradictory to partlessness, according to the reasoning already stated.
Therefore, it is established that the subject (*dharmin*) here is the gross object, which is proven by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This being the case, one must determine whether the reason (*hetu*) exists or does not exist in that subject.

In that case, when a single object such as a hand is moving, how could a gross entity—which is simultaneously perceived as having both a moving and a non-moving form—not possess the conjunction of contradictory properties?
For between two forms, one moving and one non-moving, there exists a contradiction based on their mutual exclusion;
indeed, contradiction consists precisely in the nature of mutual exclusion between existence and non-existence.
However, in the case of an entity, [its existence] is established precisely through its non-deviation from the absence of that [other].
And here, perception itself, by apprehending form as both mobile and immobile, establishes their mutual absence by implication.
But it is non-perception, without qualification, that brings about conventional usage.
It might be argued that when a single part, such as the hand, is moving, the movement of the whole should not be admitted;
for at that time, it is only the part that is seen to possess action.
And this [objection] should not be considered [as a valid refutation].
When a part possesses action, the whole which is contained within it must also possess action,
just as when a chariot moves, the person mounted upon it also moves;
for the causes of the action of the parts and the action of the whole are distinct.
And because the signs [of mental states] do not occur simultaneously:
for when there arises in the self the desire to move the hand, from that [desire] follows effort (*prayatna*).
Then, from the conjunction of the self and the hand accompanied by effort, action occurs in the hand.

But when a specific effort arises in the self for the purpose of shaking the body, then, from the conjunction of that effort-possessing self and the body, action occurs in the body; such is the difference in the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
Therefore, they are distinct. When one [of two things] has arisen, how could the other—which depends on a different cause—also arise in that same manner in the absence of that [specific] cause?
However, in the case of the chariot and the action mounted upon it, despite the difference in their causes, there is coexistence because the causes occur simultaneously.
For instance, impulsion (*nodana*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the chariot's action.
However, for the action mounted upon that [substance], there is no conjunction with motion;
and because those two [the substance and its action] coexist, the two actions also arise simultaneously.
Having considered all this, the Venerable Dharmottara stated as follows:
Moreover, a part is not possessed of action;
for when parts possess action, disjunction arises,
because action is the independent cause with respect to the initiation of disjunction.
And when that conjunction, which is the non-inherent cause, ceases, the composite substance would also cease;
this is what the disciples of Kaṇāda say in this regard:
"A specific action arising from either impulsion or impact is observed to produce a disjunction that is the opposite of the conjunction that initiates a substance."
But another [type of action] initiates mere disjunction and not the aforementioned specific [quality];
for in other actions, such as the closing and opening of a lotus, the cessation of conjunction among the parts is not observed.
Likewise, even an action produced by effort lacks the capacity to bring about the cessation of conjunction.
Therefore, there is no cessation of the substance;
this is the resolution here:
in this case, when the whole possesses action, it must necessarily be that the parts also possess action.

Otherwise, there would have to be disjunction from those points of space occupied by the parts and conjunction with those points of space not occupied by the parts for the whole— which possesses action—
whereas the parts themselves, being devoid of action, would neither withdraw from the previously occupied points of space nor connect with the points of space already occupied by the whole.
Nor can the conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts be said to arise from the conjunctions and disjunctions of the whole,
because it is not admitted that the conjunctions and disjunctions of the effect serve as the instrumental causes for the conjunctions and disjunctions of the cause;
rather, it is the conjunctions and disjunctions of the cause alone that originate the conjunctions and disjunctions of the effect.
Nor can the opposite be maintained, for that would entail the loss of one's own established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

Consequently, since parts and the whole would occupy different locations, the relationship of the supported and the support (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) would be lost, and thus even inherence (*samavāya*) could not be established.
Therefore, even if they do not wish it, the Vaiśeṣikas must accept this: when the whole possesses action, the parts possess action as well.

Just as the constituent parts must possess motion when the whole possesses motion, so too, when the parts possess motion, their own constituent parts must likewise possess motion. Following this line of reasoning, if a dyad (dvyaṇuka) possesses motion, its two originating atoms must be considered to possess motion;
therefore, the atoms connected to moving parts are themselves moving.
However, [if] that which is connected to inactive parts were itself inactive,
then even a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) substance composed of those [parts] would necessarily follow as being active when there is activity in the atoms;
for the activity of every part is invariably concomitant with the activity of the effect.

If it is argued that action belongs to one atom but not to another, then those two atoms— one active and one inactive— would become mutually separated; consequently, they would abandon the conjunction that initiates a substance,
and thus the destruction of the substance would follow.

And thus, if a binary compound (*dvyaṇuka*) possessed motion, there would be motion in the tertiary compound (*tryaṇuka*) as well; by this sequence, even a visible part would become mobile when it is actually immobile.

Therefore, atoms—which are devoid of motion because they are connected to parts that are themselves devoid of motion—would, upon being separated from those moving parts with which they were connected, undergo the destruction of the conjunctions that initiate substances.
For the atom is partless; having traversed a space of the size of a single atom within the ether, it conjoins with another atom.
Then, as it undergoes division, how could it remain without abandoning its proximity to other atoms?
For an entity possessing parts, while conjoined with one part to another object, would— by means of its other moving parts—
leave behind the previously occupied portion of space and occupy another location.
However, since this discourse is utterly inapplicable to partless entities, we perceive that it would entail the undesirable consequence of the destruction of the substance.
Alternatively, this conjunction of contradictory properties occurs in another way:
for when one part, such as a hand, is covered, the two simultaneous states of the gross object—being covered and being uncovered—inform us of its conjunction with two contradictory properties.
Nor can it be said that this [object] possesses only an unobstructed form; for even when one part is obstructed, it would follow— just as before— that the unobstructed part would still be perceived,
since perception depends upon the observation of its constituent parts.
If it is argued that its "vision" consists in the vision of that [object],
then let its nature simply be non-vision;
it should not be both vision and non-vision.
"But surely, the perception of the whole does indeed occur even when its parts are concealed; so what is this undesirable consequence?
In that case, the gross object should be perceived as it was before.
To this, someone here says:

Furthermore, the contact of the sense organ with the whole (avayavin), assisted by the contact of the sense organ with the many parts (avayava), is the cause for the perception of the gross; however, when there is an obstruction, there is no contact of the sense organ with the many parts, and therefore there is no apprehension of the gross.
He too should be questioned as follows:
Is that which is called "gross" something other than the whole?
It is that very [whole] itself, pervading many [parts], that is gross.
In that case, if the whole alone is gross, [then...]
In that case, it must be considered: why is there no perception of grossness when those [atoms] are perceived?

If you argue that the specific dimension called "grossness" is a quality (guṇa) that is indeed distinct from the substance (dravya), then in that case, that substance would be perceived as entirely devoid of dimension.
However, it does not possess conjunction with one size after another;
nor is the postulation of multiple sizes for it even tenable,
because all of them are not perceived simultaneously.
Furthermore, the cessation of the perception of that which is visible is not logical.
If it is argued that its magnitude is perceived as belonging solely to the part,
then in that case, let that very part itself— conjoined with its own magnitude— be the object of direct perception at the time of obscuration, rather than the whole.
It might be argued that, due to the error caused by inherence in a single object, it is the whole itself that appears as connected with the dimension of its parts; but even this is not tenable.
For it would follow that both the part and the whole, being of equal dimension, would appear [simultaneously].
Indeed, when a large part possesses a certain dimension, that part appears as connected with its own dimension.
Furthermore, if one accepts that the whole appears as connected with its own dimension, it would follow that two wholes of equal dimension would appear [simultaneously].
Yet, there is no such appearance as described, devoid of dimension.
If it is argued that "that part appears," [the same fault remains].
It might be argued that the whole, which appears as connected with the dimension of its constituent part, appears having abandoned its own dimension.
This too is impossible to conceive, because a part devoid of dimension has never been observed.
Furthermore, due to the cause of error consisting in inherence in a single object, even a whole possessing the smaller dimension of its parts would appear [as large].
Furthermore, even an error cannot be established without a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).
In that case, it follows that the gross part itself must be directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).
Likewise, just as during the time of obstruction, let the even grosser part be directly perceived in the state of non-obstruction as well.

Since it would be impossible to perceive a gross composite object if there were no sensory contact with its constituent parts located in the middle and at the extremities, one might think: "The perception of all constituent parts is not the cause of the perception of a gross object;
rather, it is the perception of many constituent parts [that serves as the cause].
This too is not correct.

For when a mountain or similar object stands directly in front of one, the cognition of its grossness occurs through the perception of its nearer parts in the same way as it does upon seeing those situated between the near, the far, and the middle.
Therefore, as long as there is no perception of all the parts without exception, how could there be a cognition of the most gross object?
Furthermore, the parts situated between the near, the far, and the middle are not perceived simultaneously.
How, then, could a gross composite (avayavin) be perceived?
If it is argued that the gross composite is perceived when the parts of the various directions are perceived in succession, then one must consider:
what is it that is perceived at other times?

If it is argued that [the whole] is perceived through its parts, then since even the parts situated between the front and the middle are not seen simultaneously, how could the whole itself be perceptible?
Thus, neither the whole nor the parts are perceptible; consequently, nothing at all would be seen.
Thus it is established that the gross object has both covered and uncovered forms.
In the same way, a contradiction between being colored and being colorless is to be expected;
for when one [of these] is stated, the gross object, being perceived simultaneously as both colored and colorless in its form, reveals its own connection with two mutually contradictory forms.
[Objection: But surely it is only the parts that are colored, while the whole (avayavin) possesses only the single form of being colorless.
If this were so, then when a part is red, the whole would be perceived as having a non-red form;
yet it is not so.
Alternatively, redness is indeed the conjunction with the substance that is the dye.
Furthermore, when a part is conjoined with a dyeing substance, the whole must also be so conjoined by it;
for according to the established rule, that which is the effect must necessarily be conjoined with whatever is conjoined with its cause.
As for the one who says that the whole itself is merely dyed:
For indeed, when a portion of a cloth is dyed with saffron, there arises the cognition that "the cloth is dyed with saffron.
Consequently, since the whole (the cloth) is conjoined with the substance of the dye, that whole too would not manifest any other color.
For the substance of the dye, upon coming into proximity, conceals the form of the object and connects the substance with its own form.

Just as a red part, whose innate color is concealed, appears as connected with a color inherent in the coloring substance, so too, in the case of the whole which is conjoined with the coloring substance, the undesirable consequence that no other color would appear would be unavoidable. Therefore, it cannot be said that the whole is itself red.
But another resolves this by means of the non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛtti*) of conjunction;
for he says that conjunction, like sound, is non-pervasively occurring.
Therefore, a single object can be both red and not red.
He too should be questioned as follows:
"How can it be non-pervasive?
For if it were inherent in its own substratum, like color and other qualities, it would necessarily be pervasive."
And [if you argue that] non-inherence is merely a recurrence [of a property], like fragrance in non-substances;
or if you say that its occurrence is non-pervasive because of the presence and absence of conjunction in one place—
this might be so, just as even contradictory properties such as color and taste reside in a single substratum.
Likewise, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) too would have both existence and non-existence simultaneously in one and the same place.
Oh, what a manifestation of delusion!
For non-existence (*abhāva*) consists in the cessation of existence; it does not exhibit any other form apart from that cessation of existence.
And how can that which has the nature of the cessation of something exist while that very thing is present?
Or, if it were to exist, it would abandon its nature as that cessation.
For in that case, even one who sees fire might proceed toward it seeking water.
If it is argued that because fire is observed to be distinct from water, the non-existence of water is established and thus there is no [further] activity [to seek it], we reply:
let the non-existence of water be established through non-perception; nevertheless, one who desires water might still engage in action while imagining the possible presence of water.
Now, if there were water there, it would be perceived; what follows from this?
From this non-perception, the absence of water is established.
Even so, the proof of the absence of water is indeed already accepted.
Nevertheless, one who desires that [object] might still act out of the suspicion that it exists;
for existence and non-existence are observed simultaneously in the same place with respect to conjunction.
Therefore, we postulate this [conjunction] in such a way, and not according to our own whim.
Now, is non-existence perceived as consisting in the negation of existence,
or otherwise?
In that case, if non-existence is established as having the form of the cessation of existence, how could the perception of existence not be erroneous?
Furthermore, non-existence is not of the nature of a negation of existence;
it would be a mere name.
And the existence of an object does not follow from its being a mere name.
Furthermore, since there is no mutual exclusion between color and taste such that one could be defined as "color," how could that serve as a valid example here?
Nor do we admit the inherence of color and taste in a single locus.
Sound, too, is likewise non-pervasive and unestablished; how then could it be postulated for the purpose of resolving the doubt at hand?
Enough with speaking at length.
Alternatively, a gross object is perceived as occupying both that location and a non-that location;

and between those two locations, there exists a contradiction based on their mutual absence being inseparable [from them]. Therefore, the gross object possesses a conjunction of contradictory properties.
This might be asked: how is there an invariable concomitance between the mutual absence of that [object] and its non-that-location?
It is said:
here, first of all, when a single location is being delimited, the deviation from the nature of that [object] is excluded from it.
For if that [other place] were not excluded, it would follow that there is no determination of the object itself.
And just as motion is excluded, so too is the other location which possesses motion;
for if the nature of the other location were being determined, then it would have to be perceived as having precisely that form.
When a location is perceived in its own form, setting aside its relation to another location, it is determined to be unconnected with that other location.
And just as a location is unconnected with another location, so too the form pervaded by that supporting location remains uninterrupted from connection with other locations.
For how could a form pervaded by one location exist in another location where that [first] location is absent?
Just as a jar pervaded by one location does not exist in another location;
if it is argued that it does not exist there because it is not perceived in that other location, [we ask]:
how can its non-existence be established in a remote other location?
Therefore, even one who is unwilling must admit this:
namely, that a form pervading one location does not exist in another location, because it would follow that it must pervade that [other] location as well.
Even though it exists in another location where that [object] is absent, it would have to be pervaded by that location;
yet its pervasion cannot be established,
because no other parts are possible.
By this, that which someone has said is refuted: namely,
that "just as a single entity, while producing [an effect] in a location other than its own, is not contradictory."
That too is not consistent with the context;
for it is existence and non-existence alone that are contradictory by way of mutual exclusion, not two entities.
Rather, the contradiction between two entities consists in their being invariably concomitant with each other's absence.
Therefore, whatever entity possesses the quality of being excluded by another entity, that very entity is contradictory to it.
Furthermore, the capacity to exclude one effect is not invariably concomitant with the absence of the capacity for another effect;
rather, non-perception establishes the invariable concomitance between an entity and the absence of another entity.
And when a form possessing the capacity to accomplish a specific effect is apprehended, the capacity to accomplish other effects is also delimited;
thus, how could there be an absence of that [capacity]?

However, a form connected to one location, being perceived while excluding a form associated with another location, is invariably concomitant with the absence of that [other form] and is therefore contradictory to it.

Just as in the case of two objects that are extremely similar, which are perceived simultaneously and whose difference in form exists even if it is not discerned from a distance, their difference is established by relying on a contradiction determined through direct perception,
which is caused solely by their difference in location;
so too says he who speaks [as follows].

Just as a single visual consciousness operates across distinct [objects] such as the eyes and so forth because its arising is dependent upon them, so too another [consciousness] that occurs in different locations will not be divided. Thus, when a contradiction based on the difference of location is posited, one who attributes a contradiction based on the difference of the cause of the entity does not demonstrate his own proficiency.
For consciousness has no location whatsoever,
because it is formless.
This might be so.
Just as there is contradiction caused by difference of location, so too there would be contradiction caused by difference of cause;
for what is the actual distinction between difference of cause and difference of location?
It has been stated here: there exists a contradiction between entities caused by their non-deviation from mutual non-existence;
this [contradiction] persists even when there is a difference of location, but not when there is a difference of cause.
For when two forms possessing different locations are perceived through mutual exclusion, [the contradiction remains].
These two [properties] do not deviate from mutual non-existence and do not possess different causes.

Thus, when the fourth instance of the association of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*)— which is based on the presence or absence of trembling, passion, and obscuration, and which is restricted to the locus of spatial distinction— is established with respect to the subject (*avayavin*), the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) of the reason is proven.
Now, its pervasion (vyāpti) with its own probandum must indeed be established.

Here, the conventional usage of difference among entities is observed to be based solely on the absence of the association of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmasaṃsarga), since it cannot be without a cause.
Because no other ground [for such usage] is observed,

the conventional practice of non-difference— which occurs even when there is a conjunction of contradictory properties— would thereby abandon its pervader, namely, the possession of a ground. Consequently, by the non-perception of that pervader, the [practice of non-difference] is excluded from that [conjunction of contradictory properties] and is pervaded by the absence of contradictory properties.
And its opposite is the association with contradictory properties;
therefore, this constitutes the ground for the perception of what is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

When its three-fold character (*trairūpya*) has been thus established, defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) find no occasion to arise. Thus it is said.

Thus, although many thorns of refutation fashioned by the wicked-minded have been overturned by me, this very path of the teacher’s method has been purified; let people proceed along it, having cast aside their envy.
And thus ends this refutation of the composite whole.
